newsitem.title: USA: US Treasuries end sharply higher on payrolls drop.
newsitem.headline: US Treasuries end sharply higher on payrolls drop.

text.p: Prices of U.S. Treasury securities closed sharply higher on Friday after the U.S. Commerce Department reported a surprising drop in non-farm payrolls for the month of September.
The employment data pointed to a substantial third quarter economic slowdown and suggested the Fed may refrain from hiking rates in the near future.
It was also a sign to many in the market that the Federal Reserve made the right decision in holding rates steady at its recent September 24 meeting.
A Reuters poll conducted after the payrolls release showed only six of 21 surveyed economists expected a rate rise at the Fed's upcoming November 13 policy meeting.
"I think a lot of November tightening (forecasts) got dropped out with the number," said Joshua Stiles, senior bond strategist at consulting firm I.D.E.A. Inc.
U.S. non-farm payrolls shrank by 40,000 in September versus a revised gain of 241,000 in August. The drop marked the first monthly jobs decrease since a 66,000 decline in January.
Over the past year, job growth has averaged nearly 200,000 a month. But in the July-September third quarter the average growth rate retreated to 145,000 a month.

Treasuries surged on the report, with the benchmark 6.75 percent 30-year bond yield reaching an intraday low of 6.73 percent. The bond ended the day up 1-3/32 at 99-31/32 to yield 6.75 percent, the lowest closing yield since August 12.
Despite the unexpected drop in the headline number, economists preached caution, citing other components of the jobs report which were less encouraging.

"There is some concern that the average hourly earnings were up more than expected," said Gary Thayer, senior economist at AG Edwards & Sons Inc. "I think the wage component is still something to watch."
Workers' average hourly earnings rose by six cents last month to $11.92 after rising five cents in August. Over the past year wages have risen at a 3.5 percent pace.
Economists also expressed concern about the unemployment rate which ticked up slightly to 5.2 percent but remains at historically low levels.
In the past, such a low rate of joblessness has been considered inflationary.
Overall however, the good news far outweighed the bad news for Treasuries. Now, analysts said, the focus will begin to shift to the fourth quarter where consumer spending will be key.
"The question we should all be asking is what the consumer is going to do in October, November and December," said I.D.E.A.'s Stiles.
Weak consumer spending curbed third quarter growth, but many analysts feel a near-term rebound is likely.

The three-month Treasury bill rate closed off two basis points at 4.88 percent. The six-month bill rate was down five basis points at 5.05 percent. The year bill rate down 11 basis points at 5.18 percent.

The two-year note closed up 9/32 at 100-09/32 to yield 5.85 percent. The five-year note traded up 17/32 at 100-21/32 to yield 6.22 percent and the 10-year note closed 25/32 higher at 103-20/32 to yield 6.49 percent.
